questions.title: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
questions.question: The inferior salivatory nucleus, via the glossopharyngeal nerve, lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion, supplies preganglionic parasympathetic innervation to which gland?

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior salivatory nucleus gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibres travelling with the glossopharyngeal nerve, then via its tympanic branch and the lesser petrosal nerve, to synapse in the otic ganglion; postganglionic fibres join the auriculotemporal nerve to supply the parotid gland. This is a distinctive single-target parasympathetic route, contrasted with the superior salivatory nucleus, which supplies the other salivary and lacrimal glands via the facial nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The submandibular gland is supplied by the superior salivatory nucleus via the facial nerve, chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion, not the inferior salivatory nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lacrimal gland is supplied by the superior salivatory nucleus via the facial nerve, greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, not the inferior salivatory nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sublingual gland, like the submandibular gland, is supplied by the superior salivatory nucleus via the facial nerve and submandibular ganglion, not the inferior salivatory nucleus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the inferior salivatory nucleus supplies parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve and otic ganglion.

questions.title: Which anticholinergic drug is used to treat drug-induced (extrapyramidal) tremor?
questions.question: A patient develops drug-induced extrapyramidal tremor after starting a typical antipsychotic. Which anticholinergic drug is used to treat it?

explanations.A: Correct. Benztropine is a centrally acting anticholinergic (muscarinic antagonist) that restores the normal dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia when disrupted by dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs, treating the resulting extrapyramidal tremor, rigidity and acute dystonic reactions. Its mechanism works by reducing the relative cholinergic excess from pharmacological dopamine blockade, rather than by directly restoring dopamine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Levodopa restores dopamine itself and is used for idiopathic Parkinson disease; it is not the treatment of choice for drug-induced tremor from dopamine-receptor blockade, since it would counteract the offending antipsychotic's mechanism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Propranolol is used for essential tremor and for the somatic symptoms of anxiety, not specifically for drug-induced extrapyramidal tremor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amantadine has some antiparkinsonian activity via dopamine release but is not the classic anticholinergic first-line agent for acute drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms.

questions.learning_objective: State that benztropine, an anticholinergic, is used to treat drug-induced (extrapyramidal) tremor by rebalancing basal ganglia dopamine-acetylcholine tone.

questions.title: Which glucose transporter do astrocytes use to take up glucose from cerebral capillary blood?
questions.question: Astrocytes, whose end-feet envelop cerebral capillaries as part of the blood-brain barrier, take up glucose from the capillary blood using which facilitative glucose transporter?

explanations.A: Correct. Astrocytes express the insulin-independent facilitative glucose transporter GLUT1 at high density on their perivascular end-feet and on the capillary endothelium, supporting the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle model in which astrocytes metabolise glucose glycolytically to lactate and export it to neurons as an additional fuel source. GLUT1 is distinct from GLUT3, the transporter that predominates on neurons themselves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. GLUT3 is the high-affinity glucose transporter that predominates on neurons themselves, not on astrocytes/endothelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent glucose transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, not the astrocyte/blood-brain barrier transporter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. SGLT1 is a sodium-glucose cotransporter found chiefly in intestinal epithelium and renal tubules, not the facilitative transporter used by astrocytes for capillary glucose uptake.

questions.learning_objective: State that astrocytes take up glucose from cerebral capillary blood via the GLUT1 transporter.

questions.title: Sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow from the spinal cord extends caudally as far as which level?
questions.question: The sympathetic (thoracolumbar) preganglionic outflow, arising from the lateral horn of the spinal cord, extends caudally as far as which spinal segment?

explanations.A: Correct. Sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow arises from preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn from T1 down to L2, the caudal limit of this column; no further preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies are found in the spinal cord below L2. This fixed T1-L2 extent underlies the paravertebral sympathetic chain's own longer cranial and caudal extensions, since ascending and descending fibres within the chain redistribute this output to targets at other levels.
explanations.B: Incorrect. S2 marks part of the sacral (parasympathetic) outflow, not the caudal limit of the sympathetic thoracolumbar column.
explanations.C: Incorrect. L5 is caudal to the true limit of sympathetic outflow, which ends at L2.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T12 is within the sympathetic outflow range but is not its caudal limit, which extends two further segments to L2.

questions.learning_objective: State that spinal sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow extends from T1 to L2.

questions.title: What type of sensory receptor is found in the cornea?
questions.question: The cornea, densely innervated by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, is supplied almost exclusively by which type of sensory receptor?

explanations.A: Correct. The cornea's sensory endings consist almost exclusively of bare (free) nerve endings rather than the encapsulated, specialised mechanoreceptors found in the skin. Because free nerve endings are predominantly nociceptors, the cornea is one of the most pain-sensitive tissues in the body, and even light touch is chiefly perceived as pain, which is the physiological basis of the protective corneal (blink) reflex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pacinian corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors detecting vibration and deep pressure in the skin and deep tissues, not the receptor type found in the cornea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Meissner's corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors detecting light touch in glabrous skin, not present in the cornea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Merkel discs are encapsulated mechanoreceptors detecting sustained pressure/texture in the skin, not the cornea's exclusively free-nerve-ending innervation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cornea's sensory receptors are free nerve endings, explaining its high pain sensitivity.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 1 CNS 2019 summer.pdf, item 17 ("receptors in cornea? *free nerve endings")

questions.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, classically in chronic alcoholics, results from deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.question: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, classically occurring in chronic alcoholics, results from deficiency of which vitamin?

explanations.A: Correct. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most classically in chronic alcoholics because of poor intake, impaired absorption and reduced hepatic storage. The acute phase (Wernicke encephalopathy) presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and ataxia from injury concentrated in the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, and can progress to the amnestic Korsakoff psychosis if untreated; because thiamine is a required cofactor for glucose metabolism, it must be given before or with IV glucose to avoid precipitating or worsening the encephalopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cobalamin (B12) deficiency classically causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and megaloblastic anaemia, not the Wernicke-Korsakoff triad.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Niacin (B3) deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia), a distinct clinical picture from Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Folate (B9) deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects in pregnancy, not the Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.learning_objective: State that Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency, classically in chronic alcoholics.

questions.title: The oculomotor nucleus is located in the midbrain at the level of which structure?
questions.question: The oculomotor (CN III) nucleus lies in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of which paired dorsal midbrain structure?

options.C: The red nucleus alone (no collicular level)

explanations.A: Correct. The oculomotor nucleus and the adjacent Edinger-Westphal nucleus lie in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, with emerging fibres passing ventrally through the red nucleus and out through the interpeduncular fossa. This is classically contrasted with the trochlear nucleus, which lies more caudally at the level of the inferior colliculus, giving the two extraocular cranial nerve nuclei distinct midbrain levels.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior colliculus level is where the trochlear (CN IV) nucleus lies, not the oculomotor nucleus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oculomotor fibres do pass through the red nucleus on their way out, but the nucleus itself is still classified at the superior collicular level, not defined as having no collicular level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The oculomotor nucleus is a midbrain, not a pontine, structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that the oculomotor nucleus is located in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus.

questions.title: Which structure is NOT present at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation in the medulla?
questions.question: On a cross-section of the medulla at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation, which of the following structures is characteristically absent?

options.C: The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior olivary nuclear complex, including its accessory olivary nuclei, is absent at the low level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation, only appearing more rostrally at the level of the sensory decussation and above. This absence is one of the standard identifying features used to recognise the pyramidal-decussation level on a medullary cross-section.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pyramids (with their decussating corticospinal fibres) are, by definition, present and indeed the defining feature at this level.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract run the length of the medulla and are present at the pyramidal decussation level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus (and their nuclei, just rostral to this level) are present in the lower medulla including near the pyramidal decussation level.

questions.learning_objective: State that the accessory olivary nuclei are absent at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation in the medulla.

questions.title: Which Rexed lamina is the posteromarginal nucleus, chiefly relaying pain and temperature?
questions.question: In the Rexed lamination of the spinal cord dorsal horn, the posteromarginal nucleus, the most dorsal layer chiefly relaying pain and temperature afferents, corresponds to which lamina?

explanations.A: Correct. Lamina I, the posteromarginal nucleus, is the thin, most dorsal layer capping the dorsal horn, receiving predominantly nociceptive and thermal primary afferent input (chiefly A-delta and C fibres) before relaying it onward into the ascending spinothalamic pathway. Its dorsal-most position, immediately beneath the dorsolateral tract of Lissauer through which these afferents first enter, is a key identifying feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lamina II is the substantia gelatinosa, immediately deep to lamina I, which modulates pain transmission via interneurons rather than directly relaying it onward.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lamina IV lies deeper in the dorsal horn and relays touch/proprioceptive information more than the dorsal-most nociceptive relay of lamina I.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lamina IX is in the ventral horn, containing motor neuron pools, unrelated to the dorsal horn's pain-relay laminae.

questions.learning_objective: Identify lamina I (the posteromarginal nucleus) as the dorsal-most Rexed lamina, chiefly relaying pain and temperature afferents.
